{{short description|An object whose endomorphisms are isomorphic to another structure}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''representation''' is a very general relationship that expresses similarities (or equivalences) between mathematical objects or [[Mathematical structure|structures]]. Roughly speaking, a collection {{mvar|Y}} of mathematical objects may be said to ''represent'' another collection {{mvar|X}} of objects, provided that the properties and relationships existing among the representing objects {{mvar|y<sub>i</sub>}} conform, in some consistent way, to those existing among the corresponding represented objects {{mvar|x<sub>i</sub>}}. More specifically, given a set {{mvar|Π}} of properties and [[relation (mathematics)|relations]], a {{mvar|Π}}-representation of some structure {{mvar|X}} is a structure {{mvar|Y}} that is the image of {{mvar|X}} under a [[homomorphism]] that preserves {{mvar|Π}}. The label ''representation'' is sometimes also applied to the homomorphism itself (such as [[group homomorphism]] in [[group theory]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/GroupRepresentation.html|title=Group Representation|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|authorlink = Eric Weisstein|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2019-12-07}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~teleman/math/RepThry.pdf|title=Representation Theory|last=Teleman|first=Constantin|date=|website=math.berkeley.edu|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2019-12-07}}</ref>

== Representation theory ==
Perhaps the most well-developed example of this general notion is the subfield of [[abstract algebra]] called '''[[representation theory]]''', which studies the representing of elements of [[algebraic structures]] by [[linear transformations]] of [[vector spaces]].<ref name=":0" />

== Other examples ==

Although the term ''representation theory'' is well established in the algebraic sense discussed above, there are many other uses of the term ''representation'' throughout mathematics.

=== Graph theory ===
An active area of [[graph theory]] is the exploration of isomorphisms between [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] and other structures.
A key class of such problems stems from the fact that, like [[adjacency relation|adjacency]] in [[undirected graph]]s, [[intersection (mathematics)|intersection]] of sets
(or, more precisely, [[disjoint sets|non-disjointness]]) is a [[symmetric relation]].
This gives rise to the study of [[intersection graph]]s for innumerable families of sets.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = McKee | first1 = Terry A. | last2 = McMorris | first2 = F. R.
 | title = Topics in Intersection Graph Theory
 | series = SIAM Monographs on Discrete Mathematics and Applications
 | year = 1999
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
 | location = Philadelphia
 | isbn = 978-0-89871-430-2 |mr=1672910 | doi=10.1137/1.9780898719802}}</ref>
One foundational result here, due to [[Paul Erdős]] and his colleagues, is that every ''n''-[[vertex (graph theory)|vertex]] graph may be represented in terms of intersection among [[subsets]] of a set of size no more than ''n''<sup>2</sup>/4.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Erdős | first1 = Paul | authorlink1 = Paul Erdős
 | last2 = Goodman | first2 = A. W. | last3 = Pósa | first3 = Louis | authorlink3=Lajos Pósa (mathematician)
 | title = The representation of a graph by set intersections
 | journal = [[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]]
 | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | year = 1966 | pages = 106–112
 |mr=0186575 | doi=10.4153/cjm-1966-014-3| citeseerx = 10.1.1.210.6950 }}</ref>

Representing a graph by such algebraic structures as its [[adjacency matrix]] and [[Laplacian matrix]] gives rise to the field of [[spectral graph theory]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Biggs | first = Norman
 | title = Algebraic Graph Theory
 | series = Cambridge Mathematical Library
 | year = 1994
 | publisher = Cambridge University Press
 |mr=1271140
 | isbn = 978-0-521-45897-9}}</ref>

=== Order theory ===
[[Dual (mathematics)|Dual]] to the observation above that every graph is an intersection graph is the fact that every [[partially ordered set]] (also known as poset) is isomorphic to a collection of sets ordered by the [[subset|inclusion]] (or containment) relation ⊆.
Some posets that arise as the [[inclusion order]]s for natural classes of objects include the [[Boolean lattice]]s and the [[order dimension|orders of dimension ''n'']].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Trotter | first = William T.
 | title = Combinatorics and Partially Ordered Sets: Dimension Theory
 | series = Johns Hopkins Series in the Mathematical Sciences
 | year = 1992
 | publisher = The Johns Hopkins University Press
 | location = Baltimore
 | isbn = 978-0-8018-4425-6
 |mr=1169299}}</ref>

Many partial orders arise from (and thus can be represented by) collections of [[geometry|geometric]] objects. Among them are the [[n-sphere#n-ball|''n''-ball]] orders. The 1-ball orders are the interval-containment orders, and the 2-ball orders are the so-called ''circle orders''—the posets representable in terms of containment among disks in the plane. A particularly nice result in this field is the characterization of the [[planar graph]]s, as those graphs whose vertex-edge incidence relations are circle orders.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Scheinerman | first = Edward | authorlink = Ed Scheinerman
 | title = A note on planar graphs and circle orders
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics]]
 | volume = 4 | issue = 3 | year = 1991 | pages = 448&ndash;451
 |mr=1105950
 | doi = 10.1137/0404040}}</ref>

There are also geometric representations that are not based on inclusion. Indeed, one of the best studied classes among these are the [[interval order]]s,<ref>{{citation
 | last = Fishburn | first = Peter C.|authorlink = Peter C. Fishburn
 | title = Interval Orders and Interval Graphs: A Study of Partially Ordered Sets
 | series = Wiley-Interscience Series in Discrete Mathematics
 | year = 1985
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 |mr=0776781
 | isbn = 978-0-471-81284-5}}</ref> which represent the partial order in terms of what might be called ''disjoint precedence'' of intervals on the [[real line]]: each element ''x'' of the poset is represented by an interval [''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>2</sub>], such that for any ''y'' and ''z'' in the poset, ''y'' is below ''z'' if and only if ''y''<sub>2</sub> < ''z''<sub>1</sub>.

=== Logic ===
In [[mathematical logic|logic]], the representability of [[universal algebra|algebras]] as [[relational structure]]s is often used to prove the equivalence of [[algebraic semantics (mathematical logic)|algebraic]] and [[relational semantics]]. Examples of this include [[Stone's representation theorem|Stone's representation]] of [[Boolean algebra]]s as [[field of sets|fields of sets]],<ref>[[Marshall H. Stone]] (1936) "[https://www.jstor.org/stable/1989664 The Theory of Representations of Boolean Algebras]," ''[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] 40'': 37-111.</ref> [[Esakia duality|Esakia's representation]] of [[Heyting algebra]]s as Heyting algebras of sets,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Esakia|first=Leo|date=1974|authorlink = Leo Esakia|title=Topological Kripke models|journal=Soviet Math|volume=15|issue=1|pages=147–151}}</ref> and the study of representable [[relation algebra]]s and representable [[cylindric algebra]]s.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hirsch|first1=R.|last2=Hodkinson|first2=I.|year=2002|title=Relation Algebra by Games|volume=147|series=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics|publisher=Elsevier Science}}</ref>

=== Polysemy ===
Under certain circumstances, a single function ''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y'' is at once an isomorphism from several mathematical structures on ''X''. Since each of those structures may be thought of, intuitively, as a meaning of the image ''Y'' (one of the things that ''Y'' is trying to tell us), this phenomenon is called '''polysemy'''—a [[polysemy|term borrowed from linguistics]]. Some examples of polysemy include:

* '''intersection polysemy'''—pairs of graphs ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''G''<sub>2</sub> on a common vertex set ''V'' that can be simultaneously represented by a single collection of sets ''S<sub>v</sub>'', such that any distinct vertices ''u'' and ''w'' in ''V'' are adjacent in ''G''<sub>1</sub>, if and only if their corresponding sets intersect ( ''S<sub>u</sub>'' ∩ ''S<sub>w</sub>'' ≠  Ø ), and are adjacent in ''G''<sub>2</sub> if and only if the [[set complement|complements]] do ( ''S<sub>u</sub>''<sup>C</sup> ∩ ''S<sub>w</sub>''<sup>C</sup> ≠  Ø ).<ref>{{citation
 | last = Tanenbaum | first = Paul J.
 | title = Simultaneous intersection representation of pairs of graphs
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | volume = 32 | issue = 2 | year = 1999 | pages = 171&ndash;190
 |mr=1709659
 | doi = 10.1002/(SICI)1097-0118(199910)32:2<171::AID-JGT7>3.0.CO;2-N}}</ref>

* '''competition polysemy'''—motivated by the study of [[ecology|ecological]] [[food web]]s, in which pairs of species may have prey in common or have predators in common. A pair of graphs ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''G''<sub>2</sub> on one vertex set is competition polysemic, if and only if there exists a single [[directed graph]] ''D'' on the same vertex set, such that any distinct vertices ''u'' and ''v'' are adjacent in ''G''<sub>1,</sub> if and only if there is a vertex ''w'' such that both ''uw'' and ''vw'' are [[arc (graph theory)|arc]]s in ''D'', and are adjacent in ''G''<sub>2,</sub> if and only if there is a vertex ''w'' such that both ''wu'' and ''wv'' are arcs in ''D''.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Fischermann | first1 = Miranca | last2 = Knoben | first2 = Werner | last3 = Kremer | first3 = Dirk | last4 = Rautenbachh | first4 = Dieter
 | title = Competition polysemy
 |journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | volume = 282 | issue = 1&ndash;3 | year = 2004 | pages = 251&ndash;255
 | doi = 10.1016/j.disc.2003.11.014
 |mr=2059526
| doi-access = free }}</ref>

* '''interval polysemy'''—pairs of posets ''P''<sub>1</sub> and ''P''<sub>2</sub> on a common ground set that can be simultaneously represented by a single collection of real intervals, that is an interval-order representation of ''P''<sub>1</sub> and an interval-containment representation of ''P''<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Tanenbaum | first = Paul J.
 | title = Simultaneous representation of interval and interval-containment orders
 | journal = [[Order (journal)|Order]]
 | volume = 13 | issue = 4 | year = 1996 | pages = 339&ndash;350
 |mr=1452517
 | doi = 10.1007/BF00405593| citeseerx = 10.1.1.53.8988
 | s2cid = 16904281
 }}</ref>
